title: High‐Energy and Long‐Life Na3V2(PO4)2F3 Cathodes via Multielement V‐Site Modulation of Local M–O/F Bonding
content:
Multielement V‐site modulation reshapes the local M–O/F bonding network in Na3V2(PO4)2F3, strengthens fluorine retention, suppresses low‐voltage Na3V2(PO4)3 impurities, and accelerates Na+ transport. The resulting cathode delivers 477 Wh kg−1, sustains 11,000 cycles, operates from −40 to 80°C, and enables stable 600 mAh‐level pouch cells.








ABSTRACT
Sodium‐ion batteries are promising for sustainable energy storage, but their energy density still lags behind lithium‐ion systems. Na3V2(PO4)2F3 (NVPF) is an attractive high‐voltage polyanionic cathode, but fluorine loss generates low‐voltage Na3V2(PO4)3 impurities that lower energy density and aggravate lattice deformation during cycling. Here, we report a multielement V‐site charge modulation strategy, realized in Na3‐δV1.9Zr0.02Ti0.02Cr0.02Fe0.02Al0.02(PO4)2F3 (ME‐NVPF). The deliberate combination of high‐valence Zr4+, Ti4+, and same‐valence Cr3+, Fe3+, Al3+ cations creates a heterogeneous M–O/F bonding network with multi‐directional electrostatic interactions enhancing lattice‐F retention that completely eliminates NVP impurities, lowers the Na+ migration barrier, and reduces unit‐cell volume variation to merely 2.87%. Consequently, ME‐NVPF delivers a record‐high energy density of 477 Wh kg−1, sustains 11 000 cycles, operates across −40 to 80°C, and is further validated in 600 mAh‐level pouch cells. This work establishes multielement compositional regulation as an effective strategy for designing high‐energy, long‐life, and all‐temperature polyanionic cathodes.

title: Covalently Locked Donor–Acceptor Block Copolymer Nanoparticles Enable Efficient, Stable and Reproducible Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
content:
To overcome the efficiency–stability trade‐off of traditional donor:acceptor blends, covalently locked all‐conjugated block copolymer nanoparticles are developed for solar hydrogen production. This strategy achieves an outstanding HER rate exceeding 120 mmol cm−2 g−1 h−1, alongside exceptional operational stability (95% retention after 96 h) and high batch‐to‐batch reproducibility, pioneering a robust organic photocatalyst design.








ABSTRACT
Organic photocatalysts with tailored properties and unique processability offer a sustainable route to solar hydrogen. To maximize light harvesting and charge generation, donor and acceptor materials are usually physically mixed to form D:A heterojunction nanoparticles (NPs). However, weakly constrained interactions can promote phase segregation, morphological evolution, and limited reproducibility. Here, we introduce an all‐conjugated donor–acceptor block copolymer, PBDB‐T‐b‐PYT, in which covalent linkage between PBDB‐T and PYT segments constrains nanoscale donor–acceptor organization and promotes intramolecular charge transfer. Compared with nanoparticles prepared from a physical PBDB‐T:PYT blend, PBDB‐T‐b‐PYT nanoparticles exhibit stronger photoluminescence quenching, more persistent charge‐associated transient absorption features, and improved photoelectrochemical charge extraction. As a result, hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) rates exceeding 120 mmol cm−2 g−1 h−1 (>450 µmol h−1) are achieved with low Pt loading (<3 wt.%). PBDB‐T‐b‐PYT NPs retained 95% of the initial HER rate after 96 h of photocatalysis. Conversely, NPs prepared from physically mixed PBDB‐T and PYT show lower activity and faster deactivation, consistent with morphology‐driven losses. PBDB‐T‐b‐PYT also maintains high performance across polymer batches, improving reproducibility. These results establish all‐conjugated donor–acceptor block copolymers as a promising design strategy for combining high activity, operational stability, and reproducibility in organic nanoparticle photocatalysis.

title: Ligand Electronics and Metal‐Site Acidity Enable High‐Voltage MOF Electrolytes for Quasi‐Solid‐State Lithium‐Metal Batteries
content:
Al‐FBDC, an intrinsically high‐voltage‐stable metal‐organic framework electrolyte designed by combining electron‐withdrawing ligands with hard Lewis‐acidic metal sites, is incorporated into NCM622 composite cathodes to reconstruct the local electrolyte environment at particle‐level interfaces. This design suppresses electrolyte decomposition, gas evolution, and cathode degradation, enabling durable high‐voltage operation of quasi‐solid‐state lithium‐metal batteries under demanding conditions.








ABSTRACT
Lithium‐metal batteries (LMBs) coupled with Ni‐rich cathodes offer high energy density for next‐generation energy storage. Their practical implementation, however, is limited by electrolyte oxidation and interfacial degradation under high voltage. Metal‐organic frameworks (MOFs) would regulate ion solvation and stabilize electrode‐electrolyte interfaces in quasi‐solid‐state electrolytes, yet the molecular origins of their oxidation stability remain unclear. Here, we identify ligand electronics and metal‐site acidity as key descriptors for high‐voltage‐stable MOF electrolytes. Electron‐withdrawing ligands lower the HOMO energy levels of MOFs, while hard Lewis‐acidic Al sites further enhance oxidation resistance. Guided by this principle, we design a perfluorinated Al‐based MOF, Al‐FBDC, featuring a high oxidation onset potential of 4.82 V (vs. Li+/Li). Incorporating Al‐FBDC into a composite cathode reconstructs the local electrolyte environment at particle‐level interfaces, thereby suppressing parasitic reactions and cathode degradation under high‐voltage operation. As a result, Li||Al‐FBDC@NCM quasi‐solid‐state cells deliver excellent long‐term cycling stability and rate performance, retaining 82% of the capacity after 200 cycles at 1 C over 3.0‐4.5 V, while maintaining robust performance even at 4.6 and 4.8 V cut‐off voltages and with controlled electrolyte loading. This work identifies a general design principle for high‐voltage‐stable MOF electrolytes and offers a practical route toward high‐energy‐density LMBs.

title: Site‐Selectively Engineered MoS2/ReS2 Heterostructures for High‐Performance Supercapacitors
content:
Layered MoS2 generally suffers from low electrical conductivity, sluggish electrochemical kinetics, and Mo dissolution in supercapacitors, which restrict its electrochemical performance. Here, an Fe‐doped MoS2/ReS2 heterostructure was designed, where Fe substitutes Mo sites while ReS2 remains intact. Such a strategy regulates the local electronic structure of the MoS2 domain, strengthens Mo─S bonds, suppresses Mo dissolution, and enhances electron/ion transport, leading to improved electrochemical performance.








ABSTRACT
Layered MoS2 holds great potential for supercapacitors; however, its intrinsically low electrical conductivity, sluggish electrochemical kinetics, and susceptibility to Mo dissolution severely hamper its electrochemical performance. Here, we propose a selective‐doping‐coupled heterostructure engineering strategy, in which atomic Fe preferentially incorporates into the MoS2 domain, while the local structure of the ReS2 component remains largely preserved, forming an Fe‐doped MoS2/ReS2 (Fe‐MRS) heterostructure. Theoretical and experimental results reveal the formation of a built‐in electric field at the Fe‐MRS interface, driving electron transfer from ReS2 to Fe‐doped MoS2, reconfiguring the Mo‐S electronic structure, while simultaneously strengthening Mo─S bonds and suppressing Mo dissolution. Moreover, Fe incorporation is energetically favored at octahedrally coordinated Mo sites within the MoS2 domain, modulating the local electronic environment of the MoS2 domain and thereby facilitating coupled electron/ion transport. Consequently, the Fe‐MRS electrode delivers high specific capacitance and excellent cycling stability with a capacitance retention of 97.0% over 5000 cycles. Moreover, asymmetric supercapacitors assembled with the Fe‐MRS anode achieve a high energy density of 55.2 Wh kg−1 at 1000 W kg−1, maintaining good structural and mechanical robustness. This work offers clear guidance for leveraging selective doping to engineer heterostructures with enhanced electron‐ion coupling for advanced electrochemical energy storage systems.

title: Engineering Advanced Electrocatalysts for Energy‐Saving Zinc−Air Hybrid Batteries: Concurrent Energy Storage Coupled With Chemical Upgrading
content:
An overview of zinc−air hybrid batteries (ZAHBs) is provided, covering additive selection criteria, catalyst design, and mechanisms. It highlights the key role of ZAHBs in enabling cost‐effective energy storage with concurrent chemical upgrading or wastewater remediation. Progress in three ZAHBs (wastewater‐purified, value‐added, and redox‐mediated) employing advanced electrocatalysts via electronic, geometric, and interfacial modulation is summarized, alongside critical challenges and perspectives.








ABSTRACT
Additive‐assisted zinc−air hybrid batteries (ZAHBs) that couple favorable additive oxidation with oxygen reduction represent ideal energy storage candidates, distinguished by high theoretical energy density, reduced charging voltage, and functionality for electrochemical upgrading of organics or wastewater. Herein, a critical overview of ZAHBs is provided, commencing with the fundamental electrochemistry (including advantages, working mechanisms, cell configurations, and evaluation parameters) and the selection criteria for small‐molecule additives (including theoretical potential, solubility, stability, toxicity, and volatility). We then summarize recent progress in three categories of ZAHBs (i.e., wastewater‐purified, value‐added, and redox‐mediated), discussing alternative anodic oxidation reactions (e.g., alcohol, urea, hydrazine, and iodine oxidation) coupled with cathodic oxygen reduction, along with the underlying catalytic mechanisms. Particular emphasis is placed on catalyst design strategies spanning electronic (ligand engineering, heteroatom doping, electron delocalization, orbital hybridization, and built‐in electric field), geometric (defect engineering, curvature engineering, and nano‐confinement effect), and interfacial (high‐energy interface, heterostructure, interfacial microenvironment, and core–shell structure) modulations. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and future perspectives for advancing ZAHBs. This review offers valuable guidance for the rational design and practical deployment of next‐generation energy devices.

title: Synergy Between Controllable Sulfur Defect and NiS Cocatalyst Enabling Efficient Photoredox Coupling Catalysis
content:
Controllable sulfur defects and NiS cocatalyst on Zn3In2S6 nanoflowers synergistically promote selective vanillyl alcohol valorization and H2 evolution by enhancing charge separation, surface adsorption/activation, and interfacial electron transfer, thereby enabling efficient photoredox cooperative coupling catalysis.








ABSTRACT
Semiconductor‐based photoredox coupling of selective oxidation of vanillyl alcohol (VOL) to vanillin (VAL) with H2 evolution provides a sustainable alternative to conventional industrial VAL synthesis processes, yet its performance is often hindered by rapid charge recombination and insufficient active sites. Herein, we report a facile one‐pot hydrothermal strategy to construct NiS‐decorated Zn3In2S6 (ZIS) nanoflowers with controllable sulfur vacancies (VS) for efficient co‐production of VAL and H2. Moderate concentrations of VS regulate the surface electronic structure and act as oxidation active sites to optimize VOL adsorption. Meanwhile, uniformly dispersed NiS cocatalysts serve as efficient electron relays and reduction active sites, accelerating charge migration and promoting H2 generation. Benefiting from the interfacial synergy between VS and NiS, the optimal 1%NiS‐ZIS‐VS2 catalyst delivers an 18‐fold enhancement in both VAL and H2 production rates relative to pristine ZIS, together with excellent stability and broad substrate versatility. This work highlights the critical role of defect‐cocatalyst synergy in designing advanced cooperative photoredox catalysts for sustainable chemical synthesis.

title: Machine Learning in Liquid Electrolyte Design for Rechargeable Batteries: Addressing Fundamental Challenges
content:
This review explores how machine learning tackles critical challenges in liquid electrolyte design, including ionic transport, electrochemical stability windows, and interphase stability; systematically introduces dataset construction and feature representations tailored to electrolyte chemistry; and provides actionable design guidelines for specific issues, aiming to promote the intelligent transformation of electrolyte research and expedite the advancement of next‐generation energy storage systems.








ABSTRACT
Designing high‐performance liquid electrolytes for rechargeable batteries requires simultaneously achieving fast ionic transport, a wide electrochemical window, and interphase stability, yet these objectives are intrinsically coupled and often involve competing trade‐offs. Electrolyte optimization remains a formidable challenge for conventional trial‐and‐error approaches. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) are transforming electrolyte research into a data‐driven and increasingly autonomous paradigm for accelerated materials discovery. This review provides a comprehensive perspective on how ML methodologies are tailored to address the fundamental challenges of liquid electrolyte design. We first introduce the physicochemical foundations of liquid electrolytes alongside key ML workflows, emphasizing dataset construction and feature representation tailored to electrolyte chemistry. We then examine ML strategies for predicting and optimizing ionic transport, electrochemical window, interphase regulation, and multi‐objective optimization, highlighting representative advances and practical design principles for rational electrolyte development. Finally, we discuss current challenges, including data quality, model generalizability, and interpretability, as well as future opportunities for developing mechanism‐informed and transferable ML frameworks. By bridging machine learning with electrolyte science, this review aims to facilitate the rational design of next‐generation liquid electrolytes and accelerate the development of high‐performance rechargeable batteries.
